Lost my only child, my dear son

On April 13th 2024, I lost my only child to suicide. He was 19 years old and hung himself in his room while I was fixing dinner. I had seen him come out of his room just briefly, maybe 30 mins before I found him in his room. I cut him down and performed cpr until help arrived. I’m a nurse assistant and they took him to the hospital I worked at at the time. He was in the ICU for 3 days while they ran a whole slew of tests to determine brain damage and potential brain activity. He was found to have no brain activity. I made the choice to take my best friend, my beautiful son off of life support and donate his organs. I was a single mom and he was my only child.

text:
Lost my son Nov 2024
It’s a sad club we are all surviving in. I am doing best I can. Sorry is not enough and I wish I had better words. My son was my best friend as well although I have two more sons. I did everything I could to keep him alive. His depression was so severe. We battled back and forth. He really wanted me just to let him go and I wouldn’t. I told him I would fight as long as I was still breathing. I always knew the ending of his story. I just didn’t know the when. I do know he prolonged his life for my benefit and not wanting to devastate me. I guess it became too much and I hate the life he suffered and he deserved so much more. He was beautiful, wonderful, kind and pure of heart but saw no redeeming quality in himself. He was so lonely but the fear of rejection was so great. His greatest wish was just to cuddle with a girl one time and watch TV just so he would know what it was like. He was 25 and had never been on a date or experienced the love of a partner. He had his only friend, his dog. My son lived a sad life and as his mother I am glad he is free now that I know the true depth of his pain. I have his pain now and I miss him so much it physically hurts

Lost my only child, my dear son

On April 13th 2024, I lost my only child to suicide. He was 19 years old and hung himself in his room while I was fixing dinner. I had seen him come out of his room just briefly, maybe 30 mins before I found him in his room. I cut him down and performed cpr until help arrived. I’m a nurse assistant and they took him to the hospital I worked at at the time. He was in the ICU for 3 days while they ran a whole slew of tests to determine brain damage and potential brain activity. He was found to have no brain activity. I made the choice to take my best friend, my beautiful son off of life support and donate his organs. I was a single mom and he was my only child.

text:
I’m so sorry for the loss of your son. What you’ve shared is heartbreaking, and also incredibly brave. Julia Samuel often says grief is the price we pay for love, and your words show just how deeply you loved him.

The guilt you describe is something many parents feel, but please remember guilt is a feeling, not a fact. None of us have a magic wand. However much we love them, we can’t prevent everything — we’re not God.

It means so much that in the middle of your pain you’re reaching out to help others know they’re not alone. That takes incredible courage. Sending you love and strength.

text:
i miss being casually but affectionately touched more than anything.  my husband and i were very physical; sex aside, we always touched one another.  hand resting on thigh watching TV; casually brush across shoulders as we passed each other in the kitchen; playful swat on the ass.  we were never within a foot of each other without touching in some way, for the 20+ years we were together.

i had a mammogram maybe six months after he died, and as the tech put her hand on my shoulder to gently guide me into the machine, i had a very unexpected reaction; it wasn't sexual, just the realization that no one had TOUCHED me in months, apart from sad, warm hugs. an intense physical longing is the only way to describe what i felt in that flash, and it brought flooding to me everything i was no longer experiencing.

truth be told, we'd only had sex like three times in the two years before we knew he was sick (the low T he was diagnosed with as part of his cancer explained THAT; we'd just chalked it up to him "getting older," even though he was only in his 40s and was historically a randy motherfucker - it seemed weird that he wasn't really interested beyond the release of masturbation, but i didn't want to make him feel weird about aging; turns out, that was probably what should've been our first sign something was wrong), so i was already used to living without sex.  but the casual affectionate touch, that's what i miss.  no one touches me anymore, at least not in *that* way.  and i don't get to touch anyone like that, either.

a friend of mine at the time, someone who wasn't generally thoughtful or astute, told me after he was diagnosed to hold him as much as i could.  "don't even have sex if you [he] aren't [isn't] up to it, but take the time to hold each other."

i shared her advice with him, and we took it, and i'm so grateful we did.

it's only been recently (four years on) that i find myself missing actual sex.  not in a way yet that i'd go out and look for it, but in the way that i'm finally noticing men again.  i still am thinking of the handsome guy i saw at lunch today.  a different version of me would've made an excuse to chat with him, but i'm not there yet, and i'm also not the hot slut i used to be, so despite the fact that we caught eyes a few times, i not only am not quite there, but my insecurity would've belied it anyway.

this was way more personal than i usually get about this, so i'll probably delete it, but it kind of feels good to admit all this aloud.

Obviously sex is awesome too because it’s sex and when it’s good it’s because it’s intimate and personal and with somebody you genuinely care about… I mean it’s never bad lol but it also is its own language. Sorry it’s all fucked up right now but once you hit bottom there’s only one direction to go… up. You’ll make it. I did.

I'm genuinely happy for you. I've always had the opinion that dating a widow is a thankless job. You're only with her because the man she'd rather be with is in the ground. I haven't changed that opinion just because it's now me who's a widower. Any woman I meet, will only be in my life because my love of 25 years died. I will never stop loving my wife and I will never stop thinking about her and miss her. After 25 years, 99.9% of my stuff was our stuff - stuff we bought together. I'm not about to throw out 99.9% of everything I own so another woman won't have to sit on the couch I bought with my wife.

And that's not okay. Everyone deserves to be the first choice, and to be honest, I think I'm ruined. I don't know if I'm able to fully love someone else, for fear of feeling this pain and loss again. Should I - against all odds - meet a woman who is girlfriend material, she most certainly deserves real love, deserves a better man who is not broken by grief and loss. I try to be a good man, and I genuinely think that the best I can do for such a woman is to leave her alone, free to meet someone else, someone who will give her the love she deserves.

I’m very sorry for your loss, the loss of your loved one, and your loss and isolation from the intimacy you shared.

I lost my wife of 39 years four years ago on September 1 of this year, i’m getting better and doing things that I want to do and enjoying them, but with one caveat.

I have not been intimate with anyone in a loving or sexual way since then, and that is bearing down on me quite hard. There are a couple people I would love to start dating, but I don’t know if they would reciprocate and the fear of rejection in me is strong. Very strong. I think that’s because I was the youngest child in my family and watched all my siblings eventually leave home and go off to start their own lives. My mother and father also separated and divorced between the ages of 15 and 16. Those memories are also so hard.

You don’t say how long ago it was that you lost your loved one, but in a sense time is such a fucking illusion with grief, that it doesn’t really matter. I mean it does matter don’t take that as crudeness please, it’s simply my perception.

I definitely crave intimacy with someone I can truly love and that can reciprocate, I’m not interested in sex for the sake of sex, I have to love and understand the person for that to be meaningful.

I wish you much progress in that direction, whatever direction you may choose.

Today Is Awful

My 4yo got really angry this morning. He started off opening presents and then got really quiet and then stopped all together. His brother went to give him a present and he threw it on the ground. text:
We used to get an ornament from the mall every year that had my wife and I the first year, then us with our first kid the second, then us, first kid, and baby bump, then us, two kids, and baby bump, then us and three kids. I didn’t get one this year, or the last few. Looking for one with a dad, three kids, and an angel is too hard. But pulling out the past years’ was hard on my oldest this year. 

It’ll always be hard. But it does get a bit easier, especially compared to the first.

text: I’m having my now traditional Xmas morning cry, before I go wake up the kids. My family also forgot to take my kids shopping for me. I know they’ll all feel terrible when they find out and for sure someone will ask why I didn’t remind them. I didnt have to remind them my first year as a widow, last year I did have to bring it up (awkward and made me feel pathetic), so this year I decided not to remind them.  It’s SO not about the presents, it’s about someone knowing and loving you. It truly is “the thought that counts”, and it’s so lonely knowing that there’s nobody thinking specifically of me.  Then I feel grossly selfish for thinking that. Time to put my game face back on and try to make my kids’ Xmas a joyful one. Luckily they seem to be healing from the grief appropriately. That first year was really tough. But kids are very resilient and are constantly growing and adapting themselves physically, mentally and emotionally. I wish my psyche was still as flexible.

text:
My wife passed on Jan 18th of 2013, so I had 11 months to get used to the idea of her no longer being around for Christmas. 

I went through my birthday, our sons, her birthday, our wedding anniversary, etc., before Christmas rolled back around.

Plus our sons were grown, with their own families.

We since added 5 more grandchildren and one soon to be great grandchild.

What stings is that she's not there to enjoy them, she would have been over the moon at all the grandkids.

So yeah, Christmas is the tough holiday for me, I dont listen to "missing you " Christmas music or any Christmas music in general but I decorate for my family. 

I get it.

text:
Yeah, first Christmas for me was bad. 

My wife always bought the stocking stuff for the rest of us, and so I just had to buy stuff for hers. 

After she passed, I dropped LOTS of hints that I would be buying stocking stuffers for my adult children. But they were so used to someone else getting these that they never thought it through. 

So they were absolutely mortified when my stocking was empty in the morning. They were ready to desperately go out and get stuff at a drug store when I stopped them. 

They have not forgotten since. Christmas is still a bittersweet time, but it gets better. 

You may not believe it, but it DOES get easier over time. You never forget, but time does dull the ache a little more each day. 

My new sadness is that my kids have found partners, so now I have to accept that my children need holiday visits with other families too. It’s part of the cycle of life, I guess.

I'm right there with you. My 7 year old and I are all alone this morning. We did Santa and then gifts "from mom and dad" as she inspired some of the gifts despite passing n October. We watched videos of her and my son from his first Xmas n 2018. We will watch videos of her every Xmas to honor and remember her. I cried of course but my child has seen me cry so much the past 10 weeks has used to it. He's the strong one who hugs me and tells me we will see mom again one day. I have to believe that to be true. 

It's ok to let our kids see us grieve but I get wanting to spare them that on Xmas as much as possible. We are all in this sad group together and we will live on and survive to honor our spouses and to take care of the children. That's all we can do, survive.

text:
It's our first Christmas without my wife too. I have a 14 year-old daughter and 9 year-old nonverbal son. For the first time ever, my daughter is sleeping in on Christmas morning.   
  
I understand it. If I cried wrapping her presents, then how would she feel about waking up and opening them?   
  
They each have one present from 'Mommy Ghostie.' This ghost lives in my heart now. I try to care for her there, just as I would if she were still with us.   
  
My daughter's present from 'Mommy Ghostie' is a book on the history of opium. My daughter picked it out. She co-founded a classic literature club at school this year. She has taste.   
  
Her mother would be so proud. She loved history and despised schlock. She read an incredible amount at incredible speeds.

My son's present from Mommy Ghostie is a dapper argyle sweater. He has unusually fine, symmetric features and benefits from pretty privilege. He tends to get treated better than other children with similarly severe disabilities because of his looks.   
  
His mother felt it was important to dress him well because it helps him to get on in the world. I lack aesthetic sense, but I tried my best to find select something she would have liked.

My daughter has just woken up, and so now it is time to get through this.

text:
I’m so sorry for your loss, the holidays suck. I was always a person that was anxious before Christmas, I never really enjoyed finding gifts as I was always worried they wouldn’t like them or I was just being cheap, actually I am pretty cheap.🥹

The first one was just three months after she died, my son and daughter, and my granddaughter we’re all here for it. We gave each other gifts and if I recall correctly a few of us had gifts for my wife, their mom so that was sad.

The only good thing was we had each other to lean on. my granddaughter was 15 so basically we were all adults which made it quite different.

I just want to give you a hug for being there for your kids, a four-year-old, oh my gosh. The little one must be so intelligent and feeling the loss so hard. if I had children that age I would not hesitate to let them see me cry and see the sadness I also have, because that’s real and shielding them would do no good for them. And hopefully they would also see the recovery from the moment of deep loss and sadness, something for them to grasp on to? That’s just my opinion and I can’t imagine how I would do it other than basically making up stuff, so no offense I hope.

I just wanna say I think you did really good especially sharing it here, and the idea of getting them a sitter for a few days so you can be alone and grieve will probably be very healing for you. That is my hope, that’s all I can give you this Christmas Day.

——-

Edit: I ended my comment in a bad way. I reread it, and I read all the other comments you responded to. So many have real hope in them, this is my fifth Christmas without her, it hasn’t been good, there’s sadness most every day this month. Yesterday I was just in the pits, and I saw my daughter looking that way also. We hugged and I just said “I miss her“, that broke us both into sobbing. But only for a minute or two, then we smiled and wiped each other‘s tears off. 

I needed that, I think she needed it too because things started looking up. We open gifts Christmas Eve, and her daughter has a three-year-old so she’s a grandmother and I’m a great grandfather. It’s sad that my dear wife couldn’t have seen him born 3 years ago, but that was not to be. So, giving him a wonderful Christmas, in a huge way honors her memory. Much love to you, I just had to add this. 🙏🏻❤️🫂

text: I'm so very sorry for you and the kids. This year is my second one without my husband of 40 years. It was an ounce better than last year. I'm sorry for the children, too. You're right, no one signed up for any of it. We all want to spend our whole lives with our spouse. Like you, and even though my kids are adults, I also don't want them to see me sad. Our youngest still lives with me, and he's taking it harder than his brother and sister. While I've been quietly keeping my sadness to myself, I have been better in front of him. It's what we do. I journal to my husband daily and that has helped me quite a bit. I cry as I write and sometimes I also laugh as I write when I talk to him about the silly things we did. If you can have the kids go with family, definitely do it. You need time alone to cry, laugh or both. Try to laugh and smile as much as you can, it does help. Other than that, you are not alone. Everyone here is in the same place, although different stages. You can always come here to cry or vent or ask about what to do in certain situations. I'm here if you ever need to talk. We will always, always miss them, but we will have their memories to help keep us warm inside. ❤️‍🩹

I think this sub is better than a face to face support group. Because there’s somebody here 24-7, and you can skip the ones that hurt too much. You don’t have to maintain a calm face and listen respectfully. You can skim over certain topics without hurting anybody’s feelings. You can sit as long as you want to think about what someone has said… and then you can either comment or not comment without any pressure. You can read the sub every day or you can avoid it except for once a month at 3 AM. 

I just think this sub is extremely helpful. We’re a deeply sincere casual community that mutually supports one another.

text:
I’m so sorry for your loss my friend. Everyone in this group has experienced the same, and no one can say anything that will ever make it better. But one thing you’ll find here, is people who understand. What you have and will be going through is a very lonely place. No one will truly understand, even your wife’s close family, as they have a different relationship to her. This group has helped me understand that the emotions that i felt, and no doubt you are too, are completely normal. Everyone who loses a loved one to suicide feels guilt. It’s part of the process and unfortunately there is no getting away from it. You are going to go on a rollercoaster and your emotions can shift from guilt to anger to despair from one minute to the next. I’ve even felt happy at times that my son is no longer tortured  and is free from his pain. There is going to be a lot for you to process.  Everyone here is here for you as they were for me, and my DM’s are always open if you want to vent personally. I’m gonna leave you with 2 sayings that i’ve heard which has given me some clarity, i hope they do for you too. The first is from the celebrant who did my son’s funeral. “Losing a loved one is like losing a limb. You’ll never not miss it, but you’ll learn to live without it in time.”
The second is from someone in this group. “There are no more happy days, but there are days where you’ll still feel fleeting moments of joy, make the most of them.” I wish you the best of luck and hope you heal and find some peace, and send my condolences to you and the rest of your family.

I'm sorry! There's no words in this world that will comfort you.
My wife, the love of my life, took her life 8 months ago. We had an argument just two hours before she hung herself. The guilt will probably never go away, but that's ok.

But for now just let yourself grieve all you want.

This is gonna be hard so you'll need all the strength you need. I found this strength from the love I have for my love. I hope you'll find the same for your loved one too.

Good luck.

My husband of 7 years also shot himself through the temple, but in November, after we had a bad fight. I was in the next room and did CPR until a sherriff arrived to take over, even though I could tell he was already dead. I was told after that his gunshot wound was incompatible with life, so I can understand a lot of your pain. Maybe that will be some comfort eventually in the coming journey.

I am sorry for your loss. 

My husband of seven years (partner for almost thirteen years) left this world the same way your wife did on 10/14/25, without a note. We were happy. We had plans. He stayed up drinking and playing video games and things went downhill quickly when I asked him to come to bed. I had to leave because he was aggressive with me for the first time ever. I found him laying in the floor hours later. 

The only thing that gets me through are dreams, journaling and knowing he would want me to be happy. He used to say that he loved me the most when I was being creative, so I painted lots of things he used to say on canvas as reminders of his love. I keep several journals: One for memories, one for bad memories, one for important things, and one that is mostly filled with anything and everything I would say to my love if he was here. I have seen him in dreams as well that also feel so real. The first one was about a week after his passing, when I finally convinced my family and friends I could be in our home alone. He put a hand on either side of my face, his forehead against mine and told me it wasn't my fault until I believed him. Since then there have been six other dreams. I live for dreamworld now. 

I was seeing a therapist when he died that I couldn't afford to see after his death because I lost my insurance on day one. I found free counseling through the hospice group in my area. They have widow support groups but not groups for suicide loss. This group has helped me to see that I am not alone. I hope it does the same for you. Please seek out grief counseling if you can.

Oh my gosh… do not apologize for anything!! What you’re going through is so heavy and painful. That’s something nobody should have to experience, and if anyone is going to understand what it feels like, it’s the people in this group. 

All the question that are unanswered. The horrible memory of finding a loved one, and the gut wrenching pain of that loss is so much to deal with. It’s still so new too. Things are fresh, and shocking, and that pain will evolve over time, and each time it does, you’ll have new thoughts and feelings about it all…. And this is someplace that you’re always welcome to come share that stuff. The people here are amazing, and you’re more than welcome to vent just because you can if thats what will help you that day. 

Try to take care of yourself. You’re going through a LOT right now, and it’s important to step back and take some time for yourself, and to make sure you’re able to process all of this in a healthy way, and to do it when it’s time for that to happen. In other words, don’t bottle it up!

Your son is very eloquent. "I would be glad if the peace I have found tempers your feelings of darkness," as if he knew. Maybe he did, but he didn't live with your perspective and knowledge.

What a heartbreaking devastation for you, especially in these early raw horrible days. That he didn't know. No one can possibly know the depths of this pain and shock until they get there and I am so sorry you have that, now. 

I don't know your specific pain but I do know something similar. My son wrote, ever so logically: "I understand you'll be feeling a multitude of messy emotions and I hope you can come to terms with those" and I still can't, not really. His method was shocking and messy compared to the precise and poignant words he wrote.

There is really no way to ameliorate the pain in advance. If only there was, because I am sure our sons would have tried to give it to us.

text: That was intense. I thought of my father, who took his life Nov. 16/1996. It will be 30 years ago this year. I was 20, I'm now 50. My fathers suicide was quite complex (it involved a lot, taking $300,000 from his work as a treasurer/manager of a Credit Union of 25 years. Fled to Texas and back to Canada, on the news everyday. To a forensic hospital for a month. To ending his life 16 days later. Much more in between). He left tapes, the police took copies, but I lost mine. I listened to it once, maybe twice. I remember parts. It was very long. He left a tape for my mom, and my brother as well. He talked about so much stuff. I wish I could have had it transcribed. All our tapes were quite different, I remember that. The hardest part was when he started to cry, and had to stop the recording. That's when I lost it. For 30 years I've not gone a day with peace. It really, really sucks. I feel just like your son. But having lost my dad that way, and knowing the pain left behind, makes me keep on trucking. Life has not been easy by any means. I'm thankful for 19 years of sobriety, and doing it with my boyfriend/husband, and living a much better life together. My dad will always be 53. He may have passed already by now. But that doesn't mean the grief ends. For he'll always be 53. I know he's not in pain, that does give me peace. Yet it makes me feel guilty for not saying something when I thought this might happen. I wouldn't wish my life on my worst enemy. Your sons note feels like if my dad left just a note, it would be just like that. Taking your life must be the hardest thing to ever do, so the pain must have been so bad. It brings a bit of peace knowing my dad is free. Thank you so very much ❤️ Michelle

text:
Thank you for sharing man.

I thought it was rough, losing my fiancé to cancer 2 years ago when she was 38....I cant even imagine dealing with the loss if she had been 22. 

All I can say is keep as busy as you can, and look for signs. Im a firm believer that our loved one's presence can be found every once in a while if we keep our eyes open.

For example: My fiancé died at 7:59am on a sunny day. Once the funeral home came and picked her up, I left the hospital and walked 4 miles back home. Halfway through the walk a sudden thunderstorm developed out of nowhere (she loved thunderstorms) and drenched me for the remaining 2 miles. There was no rain forecast for that day, so I am convinced that was her. That thought honestly kept me from jumping out in front of a passing car. That walk will forever be etched in my memory.

text:
I wish I didn’t know how you feel but unfortunately all of us here do…..

As I read the end of your story I started crying. It’s been 16 months since cancer took my wife and I’m able to get in my car without looking over to the empty passenger seat or reaching out for her hand. I am able to do the laundry without crying, I am able to take the garbage out without crying and I am able to pull up to my driveway without crying. I’m not sure if being able to all do all these things without so much despair all the time is good or not.  To be honest, I feel guilty sometimes when I realize that I did something and I didn’t think about her.  

We had almost 26 years of knowing each other and almost 23 years of being married, even though I got more time with her than you got with your wife, I believe the pain is the same. I’m sorry for your lack of time with her on this planet.

The one thing I know is that time does make the feelings hurt less.  Whether that’s good or not I’m not sure.

Wishing you the best of luck on your journey.

text: So very sorry! I got to have him for 37yrs, married 30 of them. I still yearn for all the things you shared. I can’t imagine a life without the yearning, but fortunately it doesn’t hit me every day anymore. I’m still healing, but in a “better place” than when it was fresh. Every day I have to decide how I want to spend my day. If the sadness creeps up on me I just make sure to process and honor it in a healthy way, and I do my best to never dwell in any of the negativity. I want him still to be proud of me. He left behind so many people who loved and respected him. Our adult kids miss their dad greatly. I often wish it was me that was taken and not him. So I’m doing my best as his wife and their mom to carry on as he would’ve encouraged us to. We’ve had many successes since, I’m always sure to tell them how proud he’d be, how I wish he were here to witness and celebrate, so we include him anyway. He is with us always, as she is with you. Treat yourself well, she’d want you to take care. Sending virtual hugs and healing vibes ❤️‍🩹

Wonderful husband and human. My heart goes out to you on such a scale and nothing I say will ever comfort you. I just wanted you to know from a stranger here, that you did everything in your power for her and she knew that. Some losses are beyond words, and they will stay with us forever.

My husband was 49 when he passed in a heartbeat. I have no words for your young beautiful wife that you lost- i’m going to say it, life isn’t total shit sometimes - and my goodness was she beautiful. These pictures of the two of you are so gorgeous.

I don’t know how we do it really. We just do. We are conditioned to I guess, the survival instinct of humans and yet sometimes when the light of those we love so much is extinguished, it becomes a battle.

I move forward with his unconditional love willing me on, and I am determined to take every single breath that was denied him in his honour.

I am deeply sorry for your loss. She was so, so beautiful.

You are remarkable man. Be gentle with yourself. I have no doubt that is what she would want.

text:
Such a powerful story and I'm sure that it resonates with many of us here. Thank you for sharing. I too miss those daily conversations about how our day was, the gossip and just the insignificant events that kept us sharing.
I'm just coming up to a year, in September, so a lot of those types memories have come rushing back recently too.
I think that you're doing all the right things and asking all the right questions. 
There was a quote on here a while ago that said something like, 'grief is a path to be walked, not a mountain to be conquered. Sometimes we walk it alone, other times we walk it with others.' 
The other thing for me is that I see it as my responsibility to keep her memory alive, for our children, our friends and her family. That doesn't mean that I'm not going to love again, but just that I will remember the love that I shared with my wife. 
Take all the time you need, and be kind to yourself. We're all with you.

I am so sorry. I was my partner's caretaker too, and I know exactly what you mean about coming apart at the seams. It's exhausting. I was in a caretaker support group for a while, and I still feel guilty now (even though he ended up passing from something unrelated) that it was my fault he died, or that I didn't give him my best in his last weeks. Obviously we can only do the best with what we have at the time, but, you know. Grief is illogical.

I read a really good poem (Learn Your Song by Gabriel Ramirez) and the line that stuck with me was "I will not hurt myself but  / I will save myself even if it hurts."

I was just messaging my late partner last night that I missed him. I hate messaging him lately because that's what draws the grief out, but sometimes that's what I need, you know?

Hugs and love to you. This really is a terrible club to be in 🩷

I just want to say as also a fellow younger widow, my LH died when I was 24 and he 27. You’re still so young. I thought I had no opportunities left, that there wasn’t any happiness left for me now since he was gone, and that I had too much baggage in life to be successful but that couldn’t be further from the truth. I’m now turning 30 and realized this year that I was so afraid it was always going to be downhill from there. His death was traumatic and I still struggle with some of the images. 

I loved my husband so deeply, we had such great plans and then plans changed. It was a weird year when I turned 27 and then 28 and I can relate to the heartache. It’s a weird feeling to think “they never made it this far”. I decided soon after that I wasn’t going to let his death ruin any future success and happiness. That he probably had peace knowing that I would make the most out of life, he used to tell me I had “grit”. I didn’t want to take that away from him or myself. I really hope you can get to the point where you’re living for you again. It made all the difference from my perspective. It’s just took a lot of grief and talk therapy to get there. Best wishes x

text:
I think about my transition from husband to caregiver a lot. She was a poet, and near the end she couldn't write anymore. I've started to write a bit of poetry in her honour, I've found it's been helpful in processing. I wrote a poem about caregiving, so here it is (i never claimed to be a good poet, so its not great)

**It was a privilege to burn.**

To hold you as the fire crept up  
your leg and made embers in your  
chest.

For a time we fought it. We thought  
we could snuff it out.

Passing buckets grew tiring.  
The well ran dry.  
The fire grew hotter.

Then all that was left  
was to burn.

I watched it consume you   
And I saw you smile as it did.

We embraced as the fire spread.  
A bramble of kindling,  
in service to its light.

I felt it change us.  
Felt it break me,  
mould me in its image.  
I watched as it razed who you were;  
who you could become.

Then one day the fire was gone.  
And so were you.  
  
Slowly, my burns have begun to heal.  
They harden,  
contract and scar.  
But now, I've come to miss the fire.

**It was only a privilege to burn.**

Im so sorry. Also canadian and near toronto, so yes thankfully no debt, i was able to get a couple paid months off, and benefits cover regular therapy. My husband (37) and I (36) also got married while he was sick (colon cancer, caught when already stage 4) and pretty quickly. It was an incredible day, we did it exactly how we wanted. I was also his primary caregiver until he went into hospice. He was in hospice 10 days before he died and our time there was actually wonderful...family and friends showed up in a big way. It was a very special time and I'm so honoured to be the person he wanted to walk with him to the end of his time here.  I'm a different person because of that experience and it's kind of like I'm working on figuring out who I am now (it's been 6 months).

I also thought/held on hope that he might live earlier on...but then it spread to his brain and everything that followed. He started to lose control of his limbs...slowly but clearly progressively. It was the first time I saw him actually scared of his illness. Up until then, while not naive about the reality, he knew he could handle it and accepted it. 

I really love the documentary Come See Me In the Goodlight about poet Andrea Gibson, and their poetry, particularly Love Letter from the Afterlife

As a fellow young widow I feel every part of this. I can’t imagine losing your wife in your early 20s though… it seems so incomprehensible and that’s from me who was widowed at 35 also because of cancer.  
I see a lot of myself and my response to things in your post. I think saying this stuff keeps it real, alive and important even if it feels wrong or weird.  
I’m on the other side of the world but I feel more seen and understood by this post than 99% of people around me.  
Young widows are a special group. We have access to the deepest and darkest parts of what it means to be human. We shouldn’t have to but we have power and wisdom beyond our years and we know what to value and what to cut out. I won’t lie I’ve been a dick at times since my husband died and I’ve got it wrong many times but I feel now like I know exactly who I am, beyond those initial years of panic and crushing grief.   
There is no timeline, no right way. But please keep talking and sharing as you go. There is much love for you here.

text:
Just wanted to send solidarity. I was 32 when my partner/spouse passed (he was 36) due to bile duct cancer (aggressive but usually impacts folks in their 70s and 80s). Watching the person you love most wither and turn unrecognizable isn’t something I’d wish on anyone. It’s been the better part of four years now, and I still miss him all the time and am in a place where I hold oodles of gratitude for what we had, the patterns of neglect and abuse from childhood and growing up he helped me set boundaries against, experiencing healthy love, etc. 

Less than a year ago, I started dating a friend of à couple years. I know my late spouse would want me to be adored, loved, and appreciated again the way he did for me (or similar, no two people are exactly alike), and it took time for me to feel ready to be open to that. My current significant other actually traveled with me to Australia earlier this year to take some of my late spouse’s stardust, meet his community in Oz, etc (he did a working visa there in his 20s and maintained really lovely friendships with folks there). My current partner made the trip feel less heavy, like a full on adventure that honored my spouse and the purpose for the visit at multiple turns. 

All of this to say, à year out is a really hard place to be - you’ve just gone through all the firsts without her. Everyone is different, and everyone seeks something different in their lives after losing their spouse, but I sincerely hope that things feel gentler for you very soon. For me the first year was definitely the worst/hardest, but I will always and forever miss him 💜

Are there ways you can honor her around this time? Fundraise for awareness, join à group fighting for patients with her type of cancer, hold a ceremony to honor her memory and favorite things (even if you’re the sole ceremony participant)? 

Wishing for gentleness for you, and moments of joy as you honor her memory and legacy that lives on in you.

text: I’m into my 5th year as a widow. And while I have many wonderful things in my life, somedays are still hard and require a good cry. Loosing your partner cracks open something deep inside of you. After my husband died at 48, I got up the next day and everyday after that for a year and walked. I walked aimlessly day after day. It saved me. I’m sure of it. Like you, I also went to therapy. It helped me to process out loud so the grief didn’t turn ugly. I also got angry and would scream with the music cranked up in my car. I bristled at anyone who said, time heals all wounds or even suggested I would be healed. I say all this to you dear stranger, that it sucks to be on this side of the looking glass without our partners, it’s a pain only we can know. But how we move forward is up to the individual. Everyone processes differently and at their own pace. Don’t judge yourself or compare, you’re doing it your way. So, as you walk the long road, I hope over time sunrises start to warm your aching heart and her memory brings more smiles and laughter than tears. Keep telling her you love her and miss her. She can hear you. All the best to you and those who are with us in the grief/love club.

text:
There is a lot of great advice here and you are clearly doing as much as you can to survive this. Being a caregiver for our partners or spouses as they die from an illness or disease really does some deep emotional damage that can take years or even a lifetime to recover from. So we need as many life preservers as we can get our hands on.

One thing that helped me survive the early years was guided meditation. I had used the headspace app and discovered they have these therapy-like sessions dealing with topics like grief, sadness, and anxiety. The grief sessions are very tough to do, and had me in tears each step, but I believe in doing them as well as the others, I was able to at least have short breaks from my constant depression and sadness, and over the years, I was able to hear my negative thoughts or react to the triggers as much, which is one of the goals of meditation.

Here is the first session for grief. I hope you will give it chance and it can help you survive better.  [Meditation For Grief - Headspace](https://www.headspace.com/meditation/grief)

text:
Hey man.
This post really, really resonated with me brother. Its taken me a couple of days to respond, my apologies.

So one day, boss-ass dude starting off your life. There you are, absolutely crushing the game. Youve snagged a beautiful, wonderful girl, you're happy. You've got your future all figured out. You won. Ya'll are such a remarkable young couple. 21, goddamn, you got your shit settled off the bat. Wouldnt be surprised if a few exes got pretty mad seeing such aura farming photos like that if they were public😂

You had it man. That counts. But of course, thats also why you're here.
I'm 33 and 6 months out. It was sudden for me. I have so much respect for you being there through all that pain and staying strong. With these trials, you already became a man more than some do at 75, you're ready to walk forward strong brother. Robbed. But, here are more than a few people that got to have all those long years, and some that only got a blink. Honestly, we can split hairs about how bad it is to get robbed before your future happens vs. How bad it is to have a long love leave you alone with no understanding of how to go on. There isn't any clean way. This is the kind of tragedy that will make anyone wince in pain just hearing it. You'll see the awkward interactions, dont sweat them.

But im so glad you got what you did brother. Gratitude is such a good thing.

I came back to this post because I wanted to share the only thing thats got me through this time in my own mind (support from friends' family, maybe therapy, even strangers, aside)

If you ever happen to read The Raven by Edgar Allan Poe, he is also grieving the loss of his woman, hes in dramatic pain and even anger, haunted, and he asks the raven "Is there no balm in Gilead?" Which means, 'is there any fucking relief from this bullshit agony you feathery bastard?' And the answer in the poem is vaguely "nevermore", but, I find that my gilead balm is just giving the exact same kindness my wife gave to everyone she met. Help. An open heart and ear to everyone. Because you get these good moments, and most importantly, you carry the legacy. I cant start with how much of an asshole ive been most of my life. So now, I wanna do what she would have done. Some day, I'll be there for her niece when shes older, a poor replacement for that close love for sure, but, ill be there. (she was like a daughter to my wife). That keeps me going, keeps me understanding its not about me, its about learning I have a backpack on now for the rest of my life with a soul inside I need to honor, and I am going to do every beautiful thing she would have wanted done. Plant those seeds, paint that canvas, give a dog a hug. Give a struggling stranger a hug or a sandwich, anything you can do. Just give it. If she would have.

Dont worry about the future rn. It is day to day.

All the love in the world young buck. Just be yourself.

text:
I took a photo of my partner who passed, holding his hand. he was hooked up to machines, but very much gone. i also took a photo of the monitor when i saw his heart rate was 0. i wanted to know the time. it took 20 minutes or so. his heart rate was in the 140s due to the epi- and norepinephrine that kept his BP and HR going. his fingers had started to get cold. he was on life support for 4 days. his mom wanted them to do the brain death tests… i had given my opinion on day one… but.. she couldn’t be the one to say it. so finally after the tests that confirmed what we already knew, but she didn’t wanna believe, she still couldn’t tell them to take it out… and i finally got to decide. i said yes. let’s go. and the nurse and i went back to his room.. a respiratory therapist came and took the tubes out, the nurse turned off the machines. and they left. it was just him and i. which was so fitting. i didn’t realize it at the time but id always told him id be with him until the end. i just didn’t know it was his end. 

but anyway. i’m so sorry. i’m glad you have this picture though. my boyfriend used to always send me pics of his hands cause i’d told him he had pretty hands. so i have a ton of them. but i wanted that very last one… even if i had to make him hold mine… and it felt all wrong but so right at the same time. 

sending healing your way.

I wasn't with my wife when she passed. She was out of state visiting relatives and took her own life in their guest bedroom.

I didn't get to see her again until the day of her service, 27 days later. It was open casket for the first hour and I had a private viewing period before and after. As I was about to leave, I decided to take a picture of her in the casket. She was so beautiful that day, you would think she was just sleeping while being well dressed and all dolled up. 

Something told me I'd need that photo. I was really struggling with denial, and I felt like I'd need to see that to tell myself that she was gone. For the most part, that did the trick, even though I still don't fully accept the loss all these months later. Eventually, from time to time, that photo became what I needed to make myself cry when I needed to let the tears flow.
